s-wh3_dbq-high-0.essay:
From the mid-1800s to the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a great deal in scale and in method. Early observers worried about damaged forests and soils in particular places. Later scientists and governments measured the whole atmosphere and treated the environment as a global problem that needed international diplomacy. However, the change was less complete than it looks. Even Marsh in 1864 warned about the whole earth, and in the twentieth century governments kept putting economic development ahead of protecting nature even when they understood the damage.

This shift happened alongside the spread of industrialization. After the Industrial Revolution began in Britain, factories and railroads ran on coal, and later oil, and burning these fuels released carbon dioxide into the air. At the same time, imperial and commercial expansion pushed farming, logging and mining into new lands, like the American West and colonies in Asia and Africa. Because the damage grew so quickly and became so visible, writers and scientists started asking how far humans were changing the natural world.

In the nineteenth century and around 1900 most concern was about land and forests. In Document 1, George P. Marsh warns that "human crime and human improvidence" could make the earth "an unfit home" and even lead to the "extinction of the species." Marsh had been a diplomat in the Ottoman Empire and in Italy, old Mediterranean lands where hillsides had been cleared and worn down for centuries. That point of view matters, because he saw what long-term deforestation had done to these regions and worried that America would repeat it. So his global warning actually came from local observations. John Muir in Document 2 describes forest reserves threatened by "the axe and fire of the lumberman" and sheep he calls "hoofed locusts." Muir wanted the reserves protected, and the result of this kind of thinking was preservation of specific places, as when the U.S. created Yellowstone, the first national park, in 1872.

The Dust Bowl showed that this land-based damage could become a national disaster. Document 4, a 1936 photograph, shows a huge dust cloud covering the road in the Texas Panhandle. Plowing up the grasslands for commercial wheat had left the soil exposed to drought and wind. The photo was made for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency, so its purpose was to show the public and Congress how bad things were and justify government programs to help farmers and change their farming methods. In this way, the understanding moved from individual writers warning people to the government taking responsibility, as with the Soil Conservation Service created in 1935.

The biggest change was the move to an atmospheric and planetary view. In Document 3, Arrhenius calculated that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees. But his excerpt is only a calculation and does not blame industry or ask for any policy, so in 1908 the science existed without any sense that it needed action. Document 5 shows that by 1960 scientists were measuring CO2 regularly at Mauna Loa, and it rose from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020. This steady government measuring was a new way of knowing about nature that turned Arrhenius's theory into evidence.

Still, knowing about damage did not mean stopping it. Document 6 describes Chernobyl and the drying of the Aral Sea, which was drained to irrigate cotton. It was written by the U.S. government in 1991 during the Cold War, so it may stress Soviet "neglect" to make the communist planned economy look bad, though the disasters were real. Document 7 shows that Brazil hosted the Eco-92 conference in Rio, yet its attention to deforestation "waned" afterward. Together these show that development stayed more important than conservation in both communist and capitalist countries.

Overall, understandings changed from local damage to a global, measured atmospheric problem, but the conflict between economic growth and protecting nature stayed the same throughout the period.

s-wh3_dbq-high-1.essay:
Between the mid-1800s and the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot in scale and method, but less in basic idea than it might seem. Early writers like Marsh and Muir already believed human carelessness could ruin the land, and they judged this by looking at forests and soil. By the late twentieth century, scientists measured damage to the whole atmosphere with instruments, and governments and international meetings treated the environment as a global political issue. Still, one thing stayed the same: governments kept putting economic development ahead of protecting nature, even when they knew the risks.

This change happened because of how the world economy grew. The Industrial Revolution spread from Britain to the United States, Germany and Japan in the 1800s, and factories, railroads and steamships ran on coal. Imperial and commercial expansion also pushed farming and mining into new areas, from the American West to colonies in Africa and Asia. In the twentieth century, oil and planned economies like the Soviet Union's sped up resource use even more. So more people were seeing environmental damage, and it was getting bigger.

In the nineteenth century, concern was mostly based on what people could see. Marsh warned in 1864 that the earth was "fast becoming an unfit home" and that human "improvidence" could even lead to the "extinction of the species" (Doc 1). This shows that even early on, some thinkers saw the danger as covering the whole planet and not just one place. Marsh's point of view matters here. He was a diplomat who had served in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, places where land had been farmed and cleared for thousands of years, so he could compare old worn-out Mediterranean landscapes with the young United States and warn Americans that their land could end up like that. Muir in 1901 described logging, fires and sheep, which he called "hoofed locusts," destroying the forest reserves (Doc 2). Like Marsh he judged damage by looking at it, and he wanted it protected. This fits with the founding of Yellowstone as the first national park in 1872, which showed the U.S. government starting to set land aside.

The understanding started to shift toward the atmosphere with science. Arrhenius calculated that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees (Doc 3). However, his excerpt does not blame industry or ask for any policy. It is a scientific calculation, which shows that knowing about a connection did not automatically mean people saw it as a problem yet. Meanwhile, damage on the ground got worse. The 1936 photograph of a huge dust storm in the Texas Panhandle (Doc 4) shows how plowing up the Great Plains destroyed the soil. The purpose of this photo matters, because it was taken for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency. The government wanted to show the public how bad the crisis was so people would support its programs to help farmers and change how land was used. This shows that by the 1930s the government itself saw human farming practices as the cause of disaster.

After 1950 the biggest change was measurement. The Mauna Loa data shows carbon dioxide rising every decade from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020 (Doc 5). This turned Arrhenius's theory into something people could track year by year, and it gave a planetary view of human impact.

But continuity remained in how governments acted. The Soviet Union diverted rivers to grow cotton, and the Aral Sea shrank badly, and Chernobyl in 1986 came from "insufficient regard for safety" to get energy (Doc 6). This was written by the U.S. government in 1991 during the end of the Cold War, so it may have focused on Soviet failures to make communism look bad, though the disasters really did happen. Brazil also hosted Eco-92, but attention "waned" afterward (Doc 7). So even though understanding became global and scientific, the conflict between development and nature that Muir described continued into the 1990s.

s-wh3_dbq-high-2.essay:
From the mid-1800s to the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot in scale. Early observers mostly worried about damaged forests, soils and regions, and later scientists and governments came to see human activity as reshaping the whole planet, especially the atmosphere. However, this change was not complete, because some early thinkers already warned about global danger, and the conflict between economic development and protecting nature continued through the whole period.

This change happened in the context of the Industrial Revolution, which spread from Britain to the United States, Western Europe, Russia and Japan in the 1800s. Factories, railroads and steamships ran on coal, and later oil became important, which released huge amounts of carbon dioxide. At the same time imperialism and commercial agriculture pushed farming and mining into new lands, like cash crops in colonies and the settlement of the American West. In the twentieth century, states like the Soviet Union used planned economies to industrialize fast, and after 1970 environmental issues became part of international diplomacy.

In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, most concern focused on visible damage to land. John Muir in 1901 describes forest reserves "wasted and threatened" by "the axe and fire of the lumberman and prospector" and by sheep he calls "hoofed locusts" (Doc 2). Muir was a naturalist writing a book to promote national parks, so his purpose was to persuade the American public to protect these lands, which is why he uses such dramatic language. His concern is about specific places in the West, not the whole world. The 1936 photograph of a dust storm in the Texas Panhandle (Doc 4) shows the same kind of regional damage, where plowing up the Great Plains grasslands led to soil blowing away. This photo was taken for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency, so its purpose was to show Americans how bad the crisis was and justify government programs to help farmers and change farming methods. This shows that by the 1930s the government itself accepted that human farming practices caused disasters.

There was also continuity, though, because some early writers saw a bigger picture. George Marsh in 1864 warned that the earth was "fast becoming an unfit home" and that human "improvidence" could even lead to "extinction of the species" (Doc 1). So the idea that humans could harm the whole planet was not totally new. Arrhenius in 1908 calculated that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees (Doc 3). However, his excerpt just presents the science and does not blame industry or call for any policy, which shows that scientific understanding came before political concern.

By the late twentieth century, the understanding had become global and was backed by measurement. The Mauna Loa data show carbon dioxide rising from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020 (Doc 5), which proves Arrhenius's idea was becoming real. Governments also responded internationally. In 1987 the Montreal Protocol was signed to phase out CFCs that were destroying the ozone layer, showing that countries accepted that human chemicals could damage the atmosphere of the whole planet and agreed to act together. Brazil hosted the UN Eco-92 conference in Rio de Janeiro after the Amazon's deforestation got "unprecedented international attention" (Doc 7).

Even so, understanding did not always lead to action. The Soviet Union caused disasters like Chernobyl in 1986 and the shrinking of the Aral Sea after its water was diverted to grow cotton (Doc 6). This source was written by the U.S. government in 1991 during the end of the Cold War, so it may emphasize Soviet failures to make the communist system look bad, but the disasters were real. Brazil's attention to deforestation also "waned following Eco-92" (Doc 7). This shows that the push for development kept winning over protecting nature.

In conclusion, understandings changed from local and regional concerns to a global, atmospheric view, but the warnings existed early and the tension between economic growth and the environment stayed the same.

Between the mid-1800s and the early 2000s, understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot in scale and method. This change in thinking happened alongside industrialization. Starting in Britain and spreading to the United States, Europe and Japan in the 1800s, factories, railroads and steamships ran on coal, and later oil became important too. At the same time, imperial and commercial expansion pushed farming, logging and mining into new lands like the American West. As burning fossil fuels and clearing land grew, the effects got bigger and easier to see, which made people rethink how much power humans had over nature.

In the nineteenth century, concern was mainly about land and the damage people could see. John Muir in 1901 described the forest reserves as "sadly wasted and threatened" by lumbermen, prospectors and sheep, which he called "hoofed locusts." Muir was a naturalist who wanted the reserves protected, so his purpose was to persuade American readers to support preservation, which is why he uses dramatic language. His focus is on specific places being destroyed by grazing and fire. The United States had already created Yellowstone as the first national park in 1872, which shows that people in this period thought the answer was to set aside certain areas. The Dust Bowl photograph from 1936 (Doc 4) also shows damage to land, with huge dust clouds over a flat plain after farmers plowed up the grasslands. Since the photo was made for the Resettlement Administration, a New Deal agency, its purpose was probably to show the disaster so the public would support government programs for farmers. That suggests that by the 1930s the government saw environmental damage as something it should step in and fix.

Still, the early period was not only about local problems. Marsh in 1864 warned that the earth itself was "fast becoming an unfit home" and that human "improvidence" could even lead to "extinction of the species." Marsh had worked as a diplomat in the Ottoman Empire and Italy, where he could see old lands around the Mediterranean that had been worn out over centuries, which may be why he thought about such long-term, large-scale damage. Arrhenius (Doc 3) also calculated in 1908 that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the earth's temperature by about 4 degrees. But his excerpt only shows calculations and does not blame industry or call for any policy, so the science of the atmosphere existed before people treated it as a problem.

By the late twentieth century, the understanding became more global and based on measurement. The Mauna Loa data (Doc 5) show carbon dioxide rising from about 317 ppm in 1960 to 414 ppm in 2020, a steady increase that proved Arrhenius's ideas were becoming real. Brazil's study (Doc 7) shows the Amazon getting "unprecedented international attention," and Rio hosting Eco-92, a UN conference, showing nature had become an international diplomatic issue.

Even so, continuity remained in the clash between development and nature. The Soviet Union drained the Aral Sea to grow cotton and suffered Chernobyl in 1986 trying to get more energy (Doc 6). Brazil's attention to deforestation "waned following Eco-92." Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the mid-nineteenth century and the early twenty-first century, but not completely. Early writers worried about forests, soil and the future of people, while later sources focused on the whole atmosphere and measured it with numbers. Still, the problem of growth and development against protecting nature never went away, so the change was large but not total.

Industrialization was going on in the 1800s.

Document 1 is by George P. Marsh in 1864. He says the earth is "fast becoming an unfit home" because of human crime and improvidence, and that people could even go extinct. This shows that already in the 1860s some people thought humans were changing the whole earth in a harmful way. Document 2 is John Muir in 1901. He describes the forest reserves as threatened by lumbermen, prospectors, sheep and fires. His concern is about forests in one country, so it is more local than Marsh. Document 3 is Svante Arrhenius in 1908. He calculated that if carbon dioxide was doubled the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees, and if it was cut in half it would fall by 4 degrees. This is a scientific way of thinking about the atmosphere, which is different from just describing damaged land. Document 5 supports this because it shows the carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa going up from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. So the idea Arrhenius had was later measured as a real rise.

The sources are not all the same kind of thing. The 1991 Soviet study was written for the United States government, so it might make the Soviet Union look bad. It talks about Chernobyl and the Aral Sea, which were disasters caused by the government's plans.

One piece of outside evidence is that Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring in 1962, which made many more people worry about chemicals and nature. This shows that understanding kept changing in the middle of the twentieth century.

In conclusion, understandings changed from local damage and warnings to scientific measurement of the planet, but the same problem of people using nature for growth stayed through the whole period.

Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between 1864 and 2020, but not completely. Early writers saw damage to forests and land, and later people saw problems that covered the whole atmosphere, yet the basic fight between using nature for money and protecting it stayed the same. So the change was large in scale and in science, but only partly in what people actually did.

The industrial revolution was going on when this period started.

In 1864 George Marsh wrote that the earth was fast becoming an unfit home for people. He said human crime and improvidence could lead to climatic excess and even the extinction of the species. This shows that worry about human impact started early and was not just about one place. In 1901 John Muir wrote about the forest reserves, which he said were threatened by the axe and fire of lumbermen and by sheep, which he called hoofed locusts. Muir is mostly talking about forests in the United States, so his concern is more about a certain kind of land than the whole planet. Both of these writers are worried about damage, but they are describing it in words and not with numbers.

The big change came with measurement. Svante Arrhenius calculated in 1908 that if carbon dioxide doubled the temperature of the earth would rise by about 4 degrees. Then the table from Mauna Loa shows carbon dioxide going from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. This shows that people went from guessing about the atmosphere to tracking it year after year. The NOAA data was collected by a government agency, and that matters because it means governments were now paying for science about the whole planet.

However, understanding did not always lead to action. The 1991 study of the Soviet Union says that Chernobyl and the Aral Sea were disasters caused by neglect in a drive for energy and cotton. That book was written for the U.S. government before the Soviet Union ended, so it may be critical of the Soviet system on purpose. The Brazil document also shows that after the Eco-92 conference the government paid less attention to deforestation even though it made a Ministry of Environment. This supports the idea that knowing about a problem did not mean it got fixed.

Outside the documents, the United States created Yellowstone National Park in 1872, which shows that some people already wanted to protect land in the nineteenth century. Later in 1988 the IPCC was created to study climate change, which shows how the concern became international.

In conclusion, understandings changed from local damage and warnings to scientific measurement of the global atmosphere, but the problem of development against conservation continued, so the change was big but not total.

s-wh3_dbq-mid-2.essay:
Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and the early 2000s, but they did not change completely. Early writers worried about damaged land and forests, while later sources focused on the whole atmosphere and on global problems, yet people kept arguing over development versus protecting nature the whole time.

The Industrial Revolution was going on when this period started.

George Marsh in 1864 already says that the earth is becoming an unfit home because of human crime and improvidence, and he warns that people could even go extinct. So the idea that humans damage the planet was not new in the twentieth century. John Muir in 1901 writes about the forest reserves and says that they are threatened by the axe and fire of lumbermen and by sheep, which he calls hoofed locusts. His concern is more about particular forests in the United States, so it is narrower than Marsh. Then Arrhenius in 1908 uses calculations to show that if carbon dioxide doubles, the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees. This is a different kind of understanding because it is about the whole atmosphere and uses numbers, though the excerpt does not say that industry is causing it or that anything should be done.

Document 5 shows the carbon dioxide measurements from Mauna Loa going up from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. This shows that the atmosphere was changing the way Arrhenius's calculations suggested it could. Document 7 about Brazil says that deforestation of the Amazon got unprecedented international attention in the late 1980s and early 1990s and that Rio hosted a UN conference in 1992. However, it also says the government's attention waned after Eco-92. This shows that even when understanding grew, action did not always follow, which supports the idea that the conflict between development and nature continued.

The Muir document was written by a naturalist who wanted the forests protected, so he has a point of view that favors conservation. Document 7 was written for the U.S. government, which is a source type that might affect what it says.

In conclusion, understanding changed from local damage to a planetary view, but Marsh already had a big view and the problems of development stayed the same, so the change was large but not total.

s-wh3_dbq-mid-3.essay:
Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and the 2020s, but not completely. Early writers worried about damaged land and forests and even about the whole earth, while later sources showed a measured, global problem with carbon dioxide. However, people kept being pulled between using nature for growth and protecting it, so the change was big in how much people knew but smaller in what was actually done.

Industrialization in the nineteenth century is the background to all of this.

Document 1 is George Marsh in 1864, and he says the earth is "fast becoming an unfit home" because of human crime and improvidence, and that people might even go extinct. This shows that some people already believed humans could ruin nature in a big way. Document 2 is John Muir in 1901, who describes the forest reserves as threatened by the axe and fire of lumbermen and by sheep, which he calls "hoofed locusts." His concern is about forests in one country and the damage from logging and grazing. Document 3 is Arrhenius in 1908, who calculated that if carbon dioxide doubled the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by 4 degrees. This is a more scientific way of understanding the problem, because it uses numbers and covers the whole atmosphere. Arrhenius does not say industry is to blame or tell anyone to do anything, though, so scientific knowledge came before political action.

Document 5 shows carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa going up from about 317 ppm in 1960 to about 414 ppm in 2020. This supports the argument that the change is global and measurable, which is different from Marsh and Muir who just described what they saw. Document 5 comes from NOAA, a government agency, which shows that governments were now measuring the atmosphere.

The documents also show continuity. In Document 7 Brazil's government paid less attention to deforestation after the Eco-92 conference even though it created a Ministry of Environment, so knowing about a problem did not mean fixing it. In the same way the Soviet Union in Document 6 had disasters like Chernobyl and the Aral Sea, which the source says came from wanting more energy and more cotton. This shows that the pull of development stayed strong in different times and places. Document 6 was written for the U.S. government in 1991, so it may have wanted to make the Soviet Union look bad during the Cold War.

An example from outside the documents is that Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring in 1962, which made many Americans worry about pesticides and helped start the modern environmental movement.

In conclusion, understandings changed from local damage to global climate science, but the conflict between economic growth and protecting nature continued, so the change was large but not complete.

Understandings of how humans affect nature changed a lot between the 1860s and today, but the biggest change was in scale. Early writers worried about forests, land and local damage, while later sources focus on the whole atmosphere and the entire planet. However, the basic problem of people using nature for economic reasons stayed the same, so the change was large but not complete.

The Industrial Revolution was happening during this time. George Marsh's book came out in 1864.

Document 1 is George Marsh's book from 1864. He says the earth is becoming "an unfit home" and that human improvidence could lead to the extinction of the species. This shows that even in the 1800s some people believed humans were seriously changing nature. Document 2 is John Muir in 1901, who describes the forest reserves as being damaged by lumbermen, fire and sheep. Muir is more focused on a specific place, the forests of the United States, and what is being lost there. Document 3 is Svante Arrhenius from 1908. He calculated that if carbon dioxide doubled the temperature of the earth's surface would rise by about 4 degrees, and that if it fell by half the temperature would drop. He was a scientist, and he does not say anything about blaming industry or making laws, he just gives numbers. So this is a new kind of understanding because it is about the whole atmosphere.

Document 5 supports this because the Mauna Loa measurements show carbon dioxide going up from 316.91 ppm in 1960 to 414.21 ppm in 2020. This shows that the idea Arrhenius had was something that could actually be measured later. Document 5 was collected by a government agency, NOAA, which shows that governments were now interested in measuring the air.

Document 7 shows that by the 1990s the problem was in international news. Brazil's deforestation of the Amazon got "unprecedented international attention" and the UN held Eco-92 in Rio de Janeiro. But the document also says Brazil's government paid less attention after Eco-92. This shows that understanding the problem did not always lead to action, which means there was continuity with the earlier conflict between development and conservation. Document 7 was written for the U.S. government, so it may look at Brazil from an outside point of view.

In conclusion, understandings changed from local worries about forests to global worries about the climate, but people still did not always act on what they knew, so the change was only partly complete.
